3.text: whistle while eating, also to laugh while an animal is being skinned.

4.text: I have previously mentioned the taboo about interchange of fire. Another

5.text: taboo of a similar kind is directed against trading off to another person

6.text: anything of long and intimate possession, — things “clinging to the heart”

7.text: (liˊñliñqin), be they of much or of trifling value. Thus, a man may trade off

8.text: a driving-sledge when it is newly made, but not after it has been in his

9.text: possession for a long time. Likewise a man must not sell the driving-reindeer

10.text: belonging to the team that he is chiefly using; but he can freely trade off

11.text: the other reindeer and the pack-sledge reindeer. This explains somewhat the

12.text: seeming contradiction between the words of Kennan, who says that he was

13.text: unable to buy live reindeer from the Chukchee,¹ and the fact that the trade

14.text: in live reindeer exists everywhere in the Chukchee territory. Kennan without

15.text: doubt wanted to buy good driving-reindeer for his personal use, which, of

16.text: course, was no easy matter. When selling a live reindeer, it is well to pull

17.text: a tuft of hair from its mane or head. If this hair is thrown into the fire of

18.text: the family’s hearth, it will prevent any part of the reindeer-luck from departing

20.text: A taboo existing among the Asiatic Eskimo forbids staying away from

21.text: one’s native land longer than five consecutive years. Here, again, the number

22.text: five has peculiar importance.² By “native land” is understood the natal village

23.text: and the surrounding territory. But the territories of more remote Eskimo

24.text: villages are considered as “alien” land. I was told by the natives, that families

25.text: who have lived for five years away from their native country must either

26.text: return, or consider themselves expatriated. In that case they must try to

27.text: establish close relations with the “spirits” of their new dwelling-place. Indeed,

28.text: though many families of Asiatic Eskimo often move from place to place, in

29.text: accordance with the vicissitudes of seal-hunting,³ they rarely go very far, and

30.text: even then they try as soon as possible to return to their native village.

31.text: Thus, most of the inhabitants of Iˊᵋen, in Providence Bay, go almost every

32.text: spring to the village of Euˊnmun, lying not far off on the shore, where the

33.text: seal-catch is more abundant, but after that they return to their own territory.

34.text: As to more distant villages, I know cases where families from Uñiˊsak, who

35.text: had staid for four years in the village of Iˊmtun, returned to their native

36.text: country in the summer of the fifth year, and vice versâ.
